paper_metadata.title: Isothermal omega Assisted Alpha Phase Precipitation and Microstructural Evolution of an Aged Ti-30Nb-3Fe Alloy

evidence.quote: In this work, the microstructure evolution of Ti-30Nb-3Fe alloy during aging heat treatments was evaluated using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction.

In a recent report, results obtained by an aging heat treatment of Ti-30Nb alloy carried out at temperatures close to 400 °C indicated that isothermal ω phase, albeit metastable, remained in the microstructure for long periods without α phase precipitation
The Ti-30Nb-3Fe (wt.%) alloy was produced by voltaic arc melting using non-consumable tungsten electrodes and a water-cooled copper crucible under a highly pure argon atmosphere.

The initial condition of the samples for all the aging heat treatments was the solution heat treatment followed by water quenching, which produced microstructures composed of β and athermal ω phases
Initially, solution heat-treated and water quenched Ti-30Nb-3Fe samples were aged at 400 ºC, applying different heating rates (1, 10 and 30 ºC/min) up to the final aging temperature.

To intensify phase precipitation and obtain a microstructure composed of fine α phase precipitates in a β phase matrix, the aging temperature was increased to 500 ºC. This heat treatment was first carried out for 30 min, 4 h, and 16 h, applying a heating rate of 30 ºC/min.

To evaluate the effects of a lower heating rate on the precipitation of α phase and its distribution in the β matrix, the same aging heat treatment was applied, but at a heating rate of 1 ºC/min. This heating rate resulted in fine and homogeneously dispersed α phase precipitates.

other.remelting: remelting and flipping the ingots several times

evidence.quote: The Ti-30Nb-3Fe (wt.%) alloy was produced by voltaic arc melting using non-consumable tungsten electrodes and a water-cooled copper crucible under a highly pure argon atmosphere. High-purity Ti, Nb and Fe elements were used as raw materials and compositional homogeneity was achieved by remelting and flipping the ingots several times.
This was followed by heat-treating the samples at 1000 ºC for 24 h with subsequent water quenching.
The resulting ingots were cold-rolled in multiple passes to decrease their thickness by up to 70% without intermediate annealing, thereby obtaining 2 mm thick plates.
These plates were annealed at 700, 800, 900 and 1000ºC for 1 h and water-quenched in order to reduce the grain size.
The initial condition of the samples for all the aging heat treatments was the solution heat treatment followed by water quenching, which produced microstructures composed of β and athermal ω phases

which produced microstructures composed of β and athermal ω phases, identified in a previous paper 11 by XRD and TEM due to small volume fraction and nanometric size of the athermal ω phase.
The nanometric ω phase was detected by XRD after only 8 h of holding time when its volume fraction was appreciable.
Note that the α phase nucleates primarily and mostly at the grain boundaries, and was also more evident after 4 h of aging time.

After 30 min of holding time at 500 ºC, the α phase precipitates were smaller than 200 nm. Increasing the holding time, even to 16 h, resulted in an increase in α lath size, which was still very small, i.e., close to 500 nm (Figure 8).
the microstructure evolution of Ti-30Nb-3Fe alloy during aging heat treatments was evaluated using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction.

The finest grain size was achieved at the lowest temperature, i.e., 700 ºC, which explains its choice for the recrystallization heat treatment. In this condition, the grain size measured by the intercept method, as specified by ASTM E112-96, was around 30 µm.
The solute rejection of Nb and Fe during the α phase precipitation led to precipitate free zones became narrower after 16 h at 500 °C and heating rate of 1 °C/min.
The strength difference between α precipitates and β matrix and consequent heterogeneous strain of phases leading a formation of microvoids on α/β interface following their coalescence.

The refinement of α precipitates was an evidence of ω-assisted α phase precipitation14, through the α phase growing on ω phase and consuming it, despite the absence of ω peaks in the XRD patterns, which was probably due to its low volumetric fraction.
